title: States of matter
objectives: Explain the origin of pressure in a gas in terms of collisions between gas molecules and the wall of the container
Understand that ideal gases have zero particle volume and no intermolecular forces of attraction
Use the ideal gas equation pV = nRT in calculations, including the determination of M<sub>r</sub>
Describe, in simple terms, the lattice structures of giant ionic (NaCl, MgO), simple molecular (I₂, C₆₀, ice), giant molecular (SiO₂, graphite, diamond) and giant metallic (Cu) crystalline solids

Describe, interpret and predict the effect of different types of structure and bonding on the physical properties of substances, including melting point, boiling point, electrical conductivity and solubility
Deduce the type of structure and bonding present in a substance from given information
prior: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding and intermolecular forces (Chapter 3)
Solids, liquids and gases and changes of state (IGCSE)
why: Why is carbon dioxide a gas but silicon dioxide a rock? Why does a balloon shrink in the fridge? This chapter connects the bonding from Chapter 3 to the behaviour you can see and measure: gas pressures and volumes, melting points, conductivity and solubility. The ideal gas equation is also one of the most reliable calculation marks on Paper 1 and Paper 2.
intro: Matter exists as solids, liquids and gases. In a gas the particles are far apart and move randomly; in a solid they are held in a regular lattice. First you will treat gases with a simple model, the ideal gas, and use pV = nRT. Then you will meet the four kinds of crystalline solid and learn to deduce a substance’s structure from its properties.

sections.title: Gases and the ideal gas model

blocks.h: Where does gas pressure come from?

Gas molecules move rapidly in random directions. Each time a molecule hits the wall of its container it changes direction, so it exerts a small force on the wall. Billions of collisions every second produce a steady force on every square metre of wall: that is the pressure.

items: More molecules in the same volume → more collisions per second → higher pressure.
Smaller volume (same amount) → molecules hit the walls more often → higher pressure.
Higher temperature → molecules move faster, hit the walls harder and more often → higher pressure.

blocks.h: The ideal gas
An ideal gas is a model that obeys pV = nRT exactly. It makes two key assumptions about the particles:

items: the particles have zero volume (their size is negligible compared with the volume of the container)
there are no intermolecular forces of attraction between the particles (collisions are perfectly elastic).

blocks.h: Real gases come closest to ideal behaviour at high temperature and low pressure. At high temperature the particles move so fast that intermolecular attractions hardly matter; at low pressure the particles are far apart, so their own volume is a tiny fraction of the total.

blocks.cap: When does a real gas deviate from ideal behaviour?
head: condition
what goes wrong with the model
effect
rows: particles are close together; their own volume is no longer negligible
actual volume larger than pV = nRT predicts
particles move slowly, so intermolecular attractions become significant
bigger particles and stronger forces (pd-pd, hydrogen bonds)
deviate more than small non-polar ones (He, H₂)

blocks.h: Helium is the most ideal of the common gases: its atoms are tiny and have only 2 electrons, so id-id forces are extremely weak.

blocks.q: Under which conditions does nitrogen behave most like an ideal gas?
blocks.why: High T: attractions negligible compared with kinetic energy. Low p: particles far apart, so their volume is negligible.

items: In an ideal gas there are no forces between the particles.
This is one of the two assumptions of the model.
Ammonia behaves more ideally than neon.
NH₃ is polar and forms hydrogen bonds; neon has only weak id-id forces.
Gas pressure is caused by molecules colliding with each other.
Pressure comes from molecules colliding with the walls of the container.

blocks.title: Ideal gas lab
blocks.h: Change the amount, volume and temperature of the gas and watch the particles. The pressure is calculated from pV = nRT. Hold the pressure constant to see the volume follow the temperature (Charles’s law), or open the solver to find any unknown with full working.

blocks.q: Calculate the volume occupied by 0.640 g of sulfur dioxide, SO₂, at 120 °C and 98.0 kPa.
blocks.err: Using 120 instead of 393 K gives a volume about three times too small.

blocks.h: Finding M<sub>r</sub> of a gas or volatile liquid
Since n = m/M, the ideal gas equation can be rearranged to give the molar mass directly:
M = mRT / pV
In the lab, a known mass of a volatile liquid is injected into a gas syringe in an oven. It vaporises completely; the increase in volume, the temperature and the pressure are recorded.

blocks.q: 0.150 g of a volatile liquid gives 52.0 cm³ of vapour at 373 K and 101 kPa. Calculate M<sub>r</sub>.
blocks.err: Converting cm³ to m³ by × 10⁻³ instead of × 10⁻⁶ makes M<sub>r</sub> 1000 times too small.

blocks.h: Changing conditions for a fixed amount of gas
If n is fixed, nR is constant, so p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂. Here any pressure and volume units may be used, as long as they are the same on both sides, but T must still be in kelvin.

blocks.q: A sealed 2.0 dm³ flask of air at 20 °C and 100 kPa is heated to 313 °C. What is the new pressure?
blocks.a: V is constant, so p₂ = p₁ × T₂/T₁ = 100 × 586/293 = 200 kPa. (Using °C would wrongly give 100 × 313/20 = 1565 kPa.)

blocks.h: Check your answer's size: 1 mol of gas at room temperature and pressure occupies about 24 dm³. If your answer is wildly different, look for a missed conversion.
A crystalline solid has its particles arranged in a regular, repeating 3D pattern called a lattice. There are four types. The key question is: what are the particles, and what holds them together?

blocks.cap: The four types of crystalline solid
head: type
particles in the lattice
forces holding the lattice together
syllabus examples
rows: strong ionic bonds in all directions
weak intermolecular forces between molecules (covalent bonds only inside each molecule)
strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure
positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons

blocks.h: Giant ionic: sodium chloride and magnesium oxide

Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions alternate in a cubic lattice. Each ion is surrounded by six ions of the opposite charge (6 : 6 coordination). MgO has the same arrangement with Mg²⁺ and O²⁻; the doubled charges make its lattice much stronger (m.p. 2852 °C vs 801 °C).

Simple molecular: iodine, C₆₀ and ice

items: Iodine: I₂ molecules (strong I–I covalent bond) packed in a regular lattice held by id-id forces. Iodine sublimes easily on gentle warming to give a purple vapour.

Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀: football-shaped molecules of 60 carbon atoms. Inside each ball the bonds are covalent, but the balls are held together only by id-id forces, so C₆₀ is soft and sublimes at about 600 °C (diamond does not melt until above 3500 °C).
Ice: H₂O molecules held in an open, tetrahedral arrangement by hydrogen bonds. This is why ice is less dense than water (Chapter 3).

blocks.h: Giant molecular: diamond, graphite and silicon(IV) oxide

head: diamond
graphite
silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂
rows: each C bonded to 4 others, tetrahedral (109.5°)
each C bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers (120°); weak id-id forces between layers
each Si bonded to 4 O; each O bonded to 2 Si
none: all 4 outer electrons in σ bonds
good along the layers: 1 delocalised electron per C

Giant metallic: copper

Cu²⁺ ions (each atom donates its outer electrons) are closely packed in a regular lattice, surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. The layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bond, so copper is malleable and ductile.

blocks.q: Match each substance to its lattice type:
Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not?
o: graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon atom
diamond has weak forces between layers
diamond is a simple molecular substance
blocks.why: In graphite each C forms only three σ bonds; the fourth electron is delocalised across the layer. In diamond all four are used in bonds.

blocks.h: To explain a property, ask: which forces must be overcome? Melting or boiling a giant structure breaks strong bonds; melting a simple molecular substance only overcomes weak intermolecular forces. To conduct, a substance needs mobile charged particles: delocalised electrons or free-moving ions.

blocks.cap: Typical properties of each structure type
head: giant ionic
simple molecular
giant molecular
giant metallic
rows: usually insoluble (unless it H-bonds with or reacts with water)

blocks.h: Deducing structure from data

items: Conducts as a solid (and liquid) → metallic (or graphite).
Conducts only when molten or dissolved → ionic.
Never conducts, very high m.p. → giant molecular.
Never conducts, low m.p. (often a liquid or gas at room temperature) → simple molecular.

blocks.name: structid
blocks.title: Structure detective
blocks.h: Each card gives data for a real substance. Use the melting point, conductivity and solubility to decide its structure, then see the explanation.

blocks.wrong: Melting iodine breaks the I–I bonds.
blocks.right: Melting a simple molecular solid overcomes only the intermolecular forces between molecules. The covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact: I₂ molecules are still present in the liquid and vapour.

blocks.q: Substance Q melts at 1083 °C, conducts as a solid and when molten, and is insoluble in water. Deduce its structure and bonding.
steps: conducts as a solid → there are mobile charge carriers in the solid: delocalised electrons
high melting point → strong bonding throughout the lattice
blocks.a: giant metallic lattice: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (it is copper)
blocks.err: Saying “ionic” because it conducts when molten: an ionic solid does not conduct as a solid.

blocks.q: Drag into order of increasing melting point (lowest first):
items: CH₄
Br₂
NaCl
MgO
diamond

blocks.q: Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride, even though both are giant ionic.
blocks.a: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double the charge of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and are smaller ions, so the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions is much stronger and more energy is needed to break the lattice.

summary: Gas pressure is caused by molecules colliding with the walls of the container.
Ideal gas assumptions: particles have zero volume; no intermolecular forces.
Real gases behave most ideally at high temperature and low pressure; small non-polar molecules (He) are closest to ideal.
pV = nRT with p in Pa, V in m³, T in K, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
1 kPa = 10³ Pa; 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³; 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³; T/K = θ/°C + 273.
M<sub>r</sub> = mRT/pV. For a fixed amount of gas, p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂.
Four lattice types: giant ionic (NaCl, MgO), simple molecular (I₂, C₆₀, ice), giant molecular (SiO₂, graphite, diamond), giant metallic (Cu).
Melting a giant structure breaks strong bonds (high m.p.); melting a simple molecular solid overcomes weak intermolecular forces (low m.p.).
Conduction needs mobile charged particles: delocalised electrons (metals, graphite) or mobile ions (molten or dissolved ionic compounds).
Graphite conducts (one delocalised electron per C) and is soft (layers slide); diamond is hard and does not conduct.
Deduce structure from data: conducts as solid → metallic; only when molten → ionic; never, high m.p. → giant molecular; never, low m.p. → simple molecular.

practice.q: Calculate the amount, in mol, of gas in a 750 cm³ flask at 35 °C and 110 kPa.
1.00 g of a gas occupies 0.574 dm³ at 25 °C and 101 kPa. Calculate its M<sub>r</sub> and suggest its identity.
Explain why ammonia deviates from ideal gas behaviour more than hydrogen.
practice.a: NH₃ molecules are larger and polar and form hydrogen bonds, so there are significant intermolecular forces; H₂ molecules are tiny with very weak id-id forces.

practice.q: Explain why silicon(IV) oxide has a much higher melting point than carbon dioxide.
practice.a: SiO₂ is giant molecular: melting it breaks many strong Si–O covalent bonds. CO₂ is simple molecular: only weak id-id forces between CO₂ molecules are overcome.

practice.q: Copper is used for electrical wiring. Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why copper conducts electricity and can be drawn into wires.
practice.a: Delocalised electrons can move through the lattice and carry charge. Layers of Cu ions can slide past each other without breaking the metallic bonding, so copper is ductile.

practice.q: Substance R sublimes at 184 °C, does not conduct in any state and dissolves in hexane but not water. Deduce its structure.
practice.a: Simple molecular (low sublimation temperature, no charged particles, dissolves in a non-polar solvent). It could be iodine.

assessment.q: Which is an assumption of the ideal gas model?
assessment.why: Ideal gas particles have zero volume and no intermolecular forces.

assessment.q: Which gas behaves least ideally at room temperature?
assessment.why: NH₃ is polar and hydrogen bonds, so intermolecular forces are strongest.

assessment.q: What volume does 1.00 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 273 K and 101 kPa?
A fixed amount of gas is heated from 300 K to 450 K at constant volume. Its pressure was 100 kPa. What is the new pressure?
assessment.why: p ∝ T at constant V: 100 × 450/300 = 150 kPa.

assessment.q: Which substance has a giant molecular structure?
assessment.why: Graphite is a giant covalent lattice of carbon atoms.

assessment.q: What is the coordination number of Na⁺ in solid sodium chloride?
assessment.why: Each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions.

assessment.q: Which forces are overcome when ice melts?
o: hydrogen bonds (and id-id forces) between molecules
assessment.why: Ice is simple molecular; O–H covalent bonds are not broken.
Graphite has delocalised electrons in its layers.

assessment.q: A substance melts at 801 °C, conducts when molten but not when solid, and dissolves in water. What is its structure?
assessment.why: Conducting only when molten means mobile ions: ionic.

assessment.q: Why is buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, softer than diamond?
o: C₆₀ molecules are held by weak id-id forces
C₆₀ has delocalised electrons between molecules
assessment.why: C₆₀ is simple molecular; diamond is a giant covalent lattice.
Delocalised electrons move through the lattice carrying charge.

assessment_s.q:
A student injects 0.100 g of a volatile liquid into a gas syringe in an oven at 110 °C. The vapour occupies 40.5 cm³ at 102 kPa.
(a) State two assumptions you make when using pV = nRT. [2]
(b) Calculate the Mr of the liquid. [3]
(c) Suggest why the experiment gives a less accurate Mr if the oven is cooler. [1]
assessment_s.a:
(a) particles have zero volume; no intermolecular forces (the vapour behaves as an ideal gas)
(b) M = mRT/pV = 0.100 × 8.31 × 383 / (102 000 × 4.05 × 10⁻⁵) = 318 / 4.13 = 77.0
(c) at lower temperature the vapour is less ideal (intermolecular forces become significant) or some liquid may not vaporise, so the measured volume is too small

assessment_s.q:
The table shows data for three substances.
X: m.p. 3550 °C, does not conduct in any state, insoluble.
Y: m.p. −7 °C, does not conduct, dissolves in hexane.
Z: m.p. 2852 °C, conducts only when molten, insoluble.
(a) Deduce the type of structure in X, Y and Z. [3]
(b) Explain the difference between the melting points of X and Y. [2]
(c) Explain why Z conducts when molten but not when solid. [1]
assessment_s.a:
(a) X giant molecular (diamond); Y simple molecular (bromine); Z giant ionic (MgO)
(b) melting X breaks many strong covalent bonds; melting Y overcomes only weak id-id forces between molecules
(c) in the molten state the ions are free to move; in the solid they are held in fixed positions

pp.skill: Choosing the correct expression for M<sub>r</sub>
pp.mis: Converting cm³ to m³ by 10⁻³ instead of 10⁻⁶
pp.stem: When 0.12 g of a volatile liquid is vaporised, the vapour occupies 64.0 cm³ at 360 K and 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa. Which expression gives the relative molecular mass of the liquid?
pp.exp: M<sub>r</sub> = m/n and n = pV/RT, so M<sub>r</sub> = mRT/pV. 64.0 cm³ = 64.0 × 10⁻⁶ m³. Value = 56.1.

wrong.D: this is m × n, not m ÷ n

pp.skill: M<sub>r</sub> of a volatile liquid from a gas-syringe experiment
pp.mis: Using the Celsius temperature
pp.stem: In a gas-syringe experiment, 0.20 g of a volatile liquid is injected into a heated syringe. All of it vaporises and the volume increases by 96.0 cm³. The temperature is 100 °C and the pressure is 101 kPa. Assuming ideal behaviour, what is the M<sub>r</sub> of the liquid?

wrong.B: T used as 100 instead of 373 K

pp.skill: Linking a gas volume to the volume of acid used
pp.mis: Using 24 dm³ mol⁻¹ when the conditions are not room conditions
pp.stem:
An excess of magnesium reacts with x cm³ of 1.50 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid.
Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)
The dry hydrogen occupies 0.962 dm³ at 100 kPa and 298 K and behaves as an ideal gas. What is the value of x?

wrong.A: assumed 2 mol acid per mol H₂ the wrong way round (halved)
wrong.C: used 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ instead of pV = nRT
wrong.D: assumed 2 mol acid per mol H₂ (as with HCl)

pp.skill: Pressure after a gas expands and is heated
pp.mis: Ignoring either the volume change or the temperature change
pp.stem: Two flasks, X and Y, are joined by a closed tap. X contains neon at 27 °C and 150 kPa. Y is evacuated and has 1.5 times the volume of X. The tap is opened and the whole apparatus is heated to 127 °C. What is the final pressure?
pp.exp: The amount of gas is fixed, so p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂. Total volume = 2.5 V. p₂ = 150 × (V/2.5V) × (400/300) = 150 × 0.4 × 1.333 = 80.0 kPa.

wrong.C: volume taken as 1.5 V instead of 2.5 V

pp.skill: Describing the sodium chloride lattice
pp.mis: Calling the particles atoms or molecules
pp.stem: Which statement about the lattice of solid sodium chloride is correct?
opts: It contains NaCl molecules held together by intermolecular forces.
Each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions, and each Cl⁻ ion by six Na⁺ ions.
It is made of sodium atoms and chlorine atoms joined by shared pairs of electrons.
Each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by four Cl⁻ ions arranged tetrahedrally.
pp.exp: NaCl is a giant ionic lattice of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a cubic arrangement. Each ion has six nearest neighbours of opposite charge (6 : 6 coordination). There are no molecules and no shared electron pairs.

pp.skill: Recognising a simple molecular lattice
pp.mis: Thinking every solid element is giant
pp.stem: Which solid has a simple molecular lattice?
pp.exp: Solid CO₂ is a lattice of separate CO₂ molecules held by weak id-id forces, so it sublimes at −78 °C. Copper is giant metallic, MgO is giant ionic and diamond is giant molecular (giant covalent).

pp.skill: Bond angles in giant structures
pp.mis: Assuming all carbon structures are tetrahedral
pp.stem: In which structure are the atoms bonded at angles of 120°?
pp.exp: In graphite each carbon is bonded to three others in a flat hexagonal layer (sp², 120°). In diamond, SiO₂ (around each Si) and CH₄, four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron (109.5°).

pp.skill: Explaining the melting points of metals
pp.mis: Describing metallic bonding as attraction between ions or shared pairs
pp.stem: Magnesium melts at 650 °C and sodium at 98 °C. Which statement explains this difference?
opts: Magnesium ions are attracted more strongly to the anions in the lattice.
Magnesium atoms share more pairs of electrons with each other.
Each magnesium atom releases two electrons into the delocalised sea and Mg²⁺ ions are smaller, so the attraction between cations and delocalised electrons is stronger.
Magnesium has stronger id-id forces between its atoms because it has more electrons.
pp.exp: Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons. Mg provides 2 delocalised electrons per atom and forms smaller 2+ ions, so the attraction is stronger than in Na (1 electron, larger 1+ ion).

pp.skill: Deducing giant covalent structure from data
pp.mis: Picking the highest melting point without checking conductivity
pp.stem: Use the data below. Which of the four substances is most likely to be a giant covalent (giant molecular) solid?
pp.exp: A giant covalent solid has a very high melting point, does not conduct as a solid or liquid, and is insoluble. D fits (it is silicon dioxide). A is simple molecular (propanone), B is ionic (conducts when molten or dissolved), C is a metal (conducts as a solid).

pp.skill: Deducing simple molecular structure from data
pp.mis: Thinking a low melting point always means a metal
pp.stem: Substances P, Q, R and S each have a different type of structure: metallic, ionic, simple molecular or giant molecular. Which substance has a simple molecular structure?

head: substance
m.p. / °C
effect of water
electrical conductivity
rows: good only when molten or dissolved

pp.exp: R melts at only 114 °C and never conducts, so it is made of molecules with weak forces between them (it is iodine). P conducts as a solid (a metal, sodium), Q conducts only in solution or when molten (ionic), S has a very high melting point and does not conduct (giant molecular).

pp.skill: Identifying a substance from its properties
pp.mis: Ignoring the change in conductivity on melting
pp.stem: A substance has a melting point of 2852 °C and a boiling point of 3600 °C. It does not conduct electricity as a solid but conducts when molten. It is insoluble in water. What is the substance?
pp.exp: Conducting only when molten means ions that become mobile: an ionic solid. The very high melting point fits small, doubly charged ions (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻). KCl is ionic but soluble with a much lower m.p.; Cu conducts as a solid; SiO₂ never conducts.

pp.skill: Matching four substances to their data
pp.mis: Not using all three conductivity columns
pp.stem: Four solids, W to Z, were tested and gave the results below. Which set of identities matches the data?
opts: W = KBr, X = CCl₄, Y = Cu, Z = SiO₂
W = KBr, X = HCl, Y = Na, Z = SiO₂
W = MgO, X = CCl₄, Y = Cu, Z = Al₂O₃
W = MgO, X = HCl, Y = Na, Z = Al₂O₃
pp.exp: W: conducts molten and dissolved, m.p. 734 °C → ionic and soluble: KBr (MgO is insoluble and melts at 2852 °C). X: liquid at room temperature (m.p. −23 °C, b.p. 77 °C), non-conducting → CCl₄ (HCl is a gas). Y: conducts as a solid with a high m.p. → Cu (Na melts at 98 °C). Z: very high m.p., never conducts, insoluble → SiO₂ (Al₂O₃ would conduct when molten).

pp.skill: Structure and bonding from properties and reactions with water
pp.mis: Assuming a soft, low-melting solid cannot be a metal
pp.stem: Substance E conducts electricity when solid and when molten, melts at 337 K and reacts vigorously with water to give an alkaline solution. Substance G does not conduct in any state, melts at 205 K and reacts with water to give an acidic solution. Which row describes the structure and bonding of E and G?
opts: E giant ionic; G giant covalent
E giant metallic; G simple molecular
E simple molecular; G giant metallic
E giant metallic; G giant ionic
pp.exp: E conducts as a solid, so it has delocalised electrons: a metal (potassium, m.p. 337 K, gives KOH). G is a non-conducting low-melting substance that is hydrolysed to an acid: a simple molecular chloride such as SiCl₄.

pp.skill: Linking electron arrangement to the structure of Period 3 elements
pp.mis: Assuming every Period 3 non-metal is giant covalent
pp.stem: X and Y are elements in Period 3. An atom of X has three unpaired electrons in its 3p sub-shell. An atom of Y has one unpaired 3p electron, and Y has a higher first ionisation energy than X. Which row describes the structures of X and Y at room temperature?
opts: X giant covalent; Y simple molecular
X simple molecular; Y simple molecular
X simple molecular; Y giant metallic
X giant metallic; Y simple molecular
pp.exp: Three unpaired 3p electrons (3p³) → X is phosphorus, which exists as P₄ molecules. One unpaired 3p electron → Al (3p¹) or Cl (3p⁵); higher first IE than P → Cl, which exists as Cl₂ molecules. Both are simple molecular.

pp.skill: Deducing a change of structure between two forms of an element
pp.mis: Thinking an element can form an ionic lattice
pp.stem: Phosphorus has two solid forms. White phosphorus melts at 44 °C, is soft and does not conduct. Black phosphorus does not melt below 600 °C, has a layered structure and is a semiconductor. Which structural change takes place when white phosphorus is converted into black phosphorus?
pp.exp: White phosphorus is made of separate P₄ molecules (weak id-id forces, low m.p.). Black phosphorus has covalently bonded layers extending through the crystal (giant covalent), so far more energy is needed to melt it. An element cannot have an ionic lattice, because there are no oppositely charged ions.

pp.skill: Completing an identification key for structure types
pp.mis: Confusing conductivity of the solid with that of the liquid
pp.stem:
A key for classifying solids uses these questions in order.
Q1: Does the solid conduct electricity? Yes → structure 1. No → go to Q2.
Q2: Does it conduct when molten? Yes → structure 2. No → go to Q3.
Q3: Is its melting point above 1000 °C? Yes → structure 3. No → simple molecular.
What are structures 1, 2 and 3?
pp.exp: Only metals (and graphite) conduct as solids → 1 metallic. Ionic solids conduct only once molten, when the ions can move → 2 ionic. A non-conductor with a very high m.p. is giant covalent → 3.

pp.skill: Properties of graphite
pp.mis: Thinking no covalent substance conducts
pp.stem: Which row describes graphite?
pp.exp: Each carbon in graphite uses three electrons in σ bonds; the fourth is delocalised across the layer and carries charge. Strong covalent bonding through the layers means graphite does not dissolve in water.

pp.skill: Comparing melting and boiling points across structure types
pp.mis: Assuming boiling points always rise with M<sub>r</sub>
pp.stem:
A student makes two claims.
Claim X: diamond melts at a higher temperature than iodine.
Claim Y: methane boils at a higher temperature than silane, SiH₄.
Which claims are true?
pp.exp: X is true: melting diamond breaks strong covalent bonds throughout a giant lattice; melting iodine only overcomes id-id forces between I₂ molecules. Y is false: SiH₄ (18 electrons) has stronger id-id forces than CH₄ (10 electrons), so silane boils higher (−112 °C vs −162 °C).

pp.skill: Ordering boiling points using intermolecular forces
pp.mis: Forgetting that branching lowers boiling point
pp.stem:
Consider these four compounds.
1 CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
2 C(CH₃)₄
3 CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH
4 CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO
What is the order of increasing boiling point (lowest first)?
pp.exp: 2 (b.p. 10 °C) is a compact branched isomer of 1 (36 °C): less surface contact, weaker id-id forces. 4, butanal (75 °C), is polar and adds pd-pd forces. 3, butan-1-ol (118 °C), forms hydrogen bonds.

pp.skill: Ideal behaviour and M<sub>r</sub> from gas data
pp.stem: This question is about helium, sulfur dioxide and an unknown gas.

parts.q: State two assumptions of the ideal gas model about gas particles.
ms: there are no intermolecular forces between the particles (collisions are perfectly elastic)

parts.q: Identify which of helium and sulfur dioxide behaves less like an ideal gas at room temperature and pressure. Explain your answer.
ms: SO₂ molecules are larger, so their own volume is less negligible
SO₂ is polar with many electrons, so it has stronger intermolecular forces (pd-pd and id-id) than He

parts.q: A sample of 0.912 g of gas Z occupies 550 cm³ at 310 K and 101 kPa. Calculate the M<sub>r</sub> of Z, assuming it behaves as an ideal gas.

pp.skill: Gas volume from a reaction using pV = nRT
pp.stem:
Sodium hydrogencarbonate decomposes when heated.
2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(g) + CO₂(g)

parts.q: Use the ideal gas equation to calculate the volume of CO₂(g) produced from 0.250 mol of NaHCO₃ at 300 °C and 101 kPa. Include units in your answer.
Suggest why the total volume of gas collected at 300 °C is larger than your answer to (a).
ms: water is also a gas at 300 °C, so 0.125 mol of H₂O(g) is also produced (total 0.250 mol of gas)

pp.skill: Conductivity and melting points explained by bonding and structure
pp.stem: Solid potassium conducts electricity. Potassium chloride conducts only when molten or dissolved.

parts.q: Name the type of bonding in potassium and in potassium chloride.
ms: potassium: metallic; potassium chloride: ionic (both needed)

parts.q: Explain how solid potassium conducts electricity.
ms: delocalised electrons move through the lattice (and carry charge)

parts.q: Explain why potassium chloride conducts when molten but not when solid.
ms: in the molten state the ions are free to move; in the solid they are held in fixed positions in the lattice

parts.q: Describe a labelled diagram that shows the metallic bonding in potassium.
ms: a regular lattice of K⁺ ions (labelled positive ions) surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons (labelled e⁻)

parts.q: The melting points of some oxides are: CO₂ −57 °C (under pressure), P₄O₁₀ 340 °C, Na₂O 1132 °C, SiO₂ 1710 °C, CaO 2613 °C. A student suggests: “An oxide melts at a higher temperature when the other element in it has a larger oxidation number.” Deduce whether the data support this hypothesis. Explain your answer.
ms: e.g. C is +4 in CO₂ but CO₂ melts far lower than Na₂O (Na +1) or CaO (Ca +2); melting point depends on structure (giant or simple), not oxidation number

pp.skill: Allotropes of carbon and the forces broken on melting
pp.stem: Diamond and buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, are both forms of carbon.

parts.q: Name the type of lattice structure in diamond and in solid C₆₀.
ms: diamond: giant molecular (giant covalent); C₆₀: simple molecular (both needed)

parts.q: Explain why C₆₀ has a much lower sublimation temperature than diamond.
ms: in C₆₀ only weak id-id forces between molecules are overcome
in diamond many strong covalent bonds must be broken

parts.q: Identify the strongest force broken when each substance melts: CH₄, NH₃, HCl, SiO₂, CaO. Use: i.d. (id-id), p.d. (pd-pd), H (hydrogen bond), C (covalent bond), I (ionic bond).
ms: SiO₂: C; CaO: I (all five correct for 3 marks; four for 2; three for 1)

pp.skill: Lattice structures and conductivity across Period 3
pp.stem: The elements of Period 3 show trends in structure and electrical conductivity.

parts.q: Identify the lattice structure of the crystalline solid of each element: aluminium, silicon, sulfur.
Explain why the electrical conductivity increases from Na to Al and why P, S and Cl do not conduct.
ms: Na → Al: more delocalised electrons per atom (1, 2, 3)
P, S, Cl: simple molecular, no delocalised electrons or ions (all electrons held in covalent bonds or lone pairs)
